msItem.incipit: Well since th’art dead if thou canst mortals hear

abstract.p: The poem mourns Mr. Davenant, an Oxford mayor who died two weeks after his wife. It notes that death is common, but the poet is especially saddened when good people die. The poet says that Davenant lived a virtuous life that needed no exaggerated praise. He had natural talents, education, honours, wealth, and children, and was fortunate in many ways. After his wife died, he lived long enough to perform her funeral rites, then died himself fourteen days later. The poem ends by addressing the couple together, wishing them a peaceful rest in their shared grave.

div.head:
On Mr Davenantt who died att Oxford in his Maioralty
A fortnight after his Wife.

lg.l: Well sceince since th’art deade, if thou canst mortalls heare,
Take this just Tribute of a Funerall teare,
Each day I see a Corse, and now no Knell
Is more Familiare then a Passing-Bell;
All die no fix'ed inheritance men have,
Save that they are freeholders to the grave.
Only I greive, when vertues brood
Becomes Wormes meate, and is the Cankers foode.
Alas that vnrelenting death should bee
At odds with Goodnesse! Fairest budds wee see
Are soonest cropp’t; Wee know the fewest crimes,
Tis theire pererogative to die bee-times
Enlargd from this Worlds misery: And thus hee
Whom wee now waile made hast to bee made free.
There needes no loud Hyperbole sett him foorth,
Nor sawcy Elegy to bely his worth;
His life was an Encomium large enough:
True Gold doth neede no foyles to sett itt off
Hee had choyce giftes of nature and of arte;
Neither was Fortune wanting on her parte
To him in Honours, Wealth, or Progeny:
Hee was on all sides blest! Why should hee dye?
And yett why should he live his mate being gone,
And Turtle like sigh out and endlesse moone?
No, no; hee loved her better, and would not so easily
So easily lost what hee so hardly gott.
Hee liv’d to pay the last Rites to his Bride,
That done hee pin’d out fourteene dayes and died.
Thrice happy paire! Oh could my simple Verse
Reare you a lasting Trophee on your your Hearse,
You should vie yeares with time; Had you your due,
Eternety were as short liv’d as you.
Farewell and in one Grave now you are deade
Sleepe undisturbd, as in your marriage beed.

div.head: Historical context and dating
div.p: John Davenant (1565–1622), vintner and proprietor of the Crown Inn, Cornmarket Street, Oxford was elected mayor on 17 September 1621. His wife Jane (née Sheppard) died on 5 April 1622 and was buried at St Martin’s Church, Oxford. Davenant died fourteen days later on 19 April 1622. His will requested burial as near to his wife “as the place will give leave where she lyeth.” The Davenants were well-known, they kept an important inn frequented by Shakespeare, and their son William became a prominent dramatist.
